newsitem.title: philippines: New Zealand boy abducted in Manila, freed.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand boy abducted in Manila, freed.

text.p: Ten gunmen with automatic rifles seized a 13-year-old New Zealand boy on Thursday in broad daylight in the main financial centre but released him and his family driver unharmed after taking their car, police said.
The gang abducted Benjamin Austin, son of a senior Asian Development Bank official, and the driver at noon in the heart of the Makati district of foreign embassies, big corporations and luxury homes.
Benjamin, whose family is from Christchurch, told Reuters that he and the driver were returning from a visit to a video store when two cars blocked their way.
"These guys with M-16 (assault rifles) and grenade launchers ... forced us to the back and to crouch down. Then they drove with us," Benjamin said.
The gunmen abandoned the pair in the Manila suburb of Pasig an hour later.
An initial police bulletin said they had been kidnapped.
Benjamin's father, John Austin, is an alternate executive director of the Manila-based bank.

"They (the criminals) are really getting more and more brazen. This suggests a total breakdown of law and order," said university professor Teresita Ang See, a leader of a citizens' group which monitors kidnappings.

"But the government only wants to cosmetise the problem, to cover it up, in the face of the APEC conference," See said, referring to Manila's role as host of next month's Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit.
APEC organisers have pledged tight security for the summit, which will be attended by leaders of 16 of APEC's 18 member economies, among them U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Austin's abduction occurred four days after gunmen tried to kidnap James Dy, president of the influential Filipino-Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, in another part of the capital.
Gunmen wearing masks blocked Dy's van but his driver swung into the opposite lane and sped away under a hail of gunfire, Chinese community sources said.
Kidnap gangs abducted a total of 114 people in the first nine months of this year and collected 36.2 million pesos ($1.35 million) in ransom, according to police statistics.
Thirty-seven of the kidnappings occurred in the Manila area.
Police and soldiers have frequently been linked to kidnap gangs and Chinese community sources say they believe these gangs operate under the protection of senior officers.
Many victims, often from the economically powerful Filipino-Chinese community, do not bother telling the police they have been kidnapped, preferring instead to pay off the ransom quickly.
The kidnappings have become so much a matter of routine that the gangs sometimes accept cheques as ransom payments.
